title: Isolated burst reservoirs and SLO-driven degradation controller
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Background: Dedicated fleets occasionally see tenant-level spikes that consume short-term capacity and cause noisy-neighbor tail latency regressions for other tenants. Existing rate-limiting and queueing is global or weight-based and does not provide a bounded per-tenant short-term burst allowance coupled to SLO-aware degradation.

Goal: Implement a per-tenant 'burst reservoir' that stores a small reserve of immediate request tokens (refillable over a defined window) combined with an SLO-driven degradation controller that gracefully demotes non-critical requests (or route to cheaper model variants) when reservoir and steady-state capacity are exhausted. The system must: (1) enforce isolation for short spikes without reducing long-term throughput guarantees, (2) integrate with existing autoscaling signals to avoid thrashing, and (3) provide observability and safe rollouts behind a feature flag.

Scope: Routing and admission layer changes for Dedicated fleets only. No changes to public API. Concurrency knobs, token accounting, and pluggable degradation policies to be added. Autoscaler hooks will be created to expose reservoir pressure metrics.

Out of scope: Changes to user-facing quota UI and pricing. Full multi-region federation of reservoirs will be a follow-up.
acceptance_criteria: Per-tenant reservoir implemented with configurable size and refill window (defaults: 1000 tokens, 60s window)
When reservoir drains, system applies configured degradation policy (drop, deprioritize to lower-weight queue, or fallback to compatible model) within 200ms of decision
Integration test demonstrating tenant A spike not causing >2x p99 increase for tenant B under mixed traffic in the staging dedicated cluster
Autoscaling integration: reservoir pressure exposed as metric and used as a soft signal (not sole) by the dedicated autoscaler; no autoscaler oscillations in 30m chaos test
Rollout: feature flag gated, canary to 10% of fleets, with automatic rollback on >10% p50/p95/regression for any tenant within 1h
notes: 2026-02-25: Spike complete. Prototype in branch feature/reservoirs using in-process token buckets per tenant. Microbenchmarks show ~12% reduction in downstream p99 for neighbors under synthetic bursts.

2026-03-01: Design reviewed by infra/serving. Key trade-off: centralized vs per-node reservoir state. Decided on per-node soft reservoirs with eventual consistency to reduce write amplification to control plane. See design doc: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/INF/pages/45210

2026-03-05: UX/PM feedback: need explicit metric mapping so users can correlate reservoir behavior to billing and throttling. Added metrics: reservoir.tokens_available, reservoir.pressure, reservoir.evictions_total.
2026-03-08: PR opened: https://github.com/redwood-inference/realtime/pull/7824 — implements core accounting and a simple drop policy behind feature flag 'reservoirs_v1'
2026-03-10: Load test plan linked: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1fJ-reservoir-load-plan — includes mixed-tenant Poisson spikes, long-tail background traffic, and autoscaler chaostest scenarios

2026-03-11: Preliminary integration in staging shows one regression: short-lived autoscaler scale-ups when reservoir drains rapidly. Engineering decision: treat reservoir_pressure as a soft signal and add a 30s debounce in the autoscaler hook to avoid reacting to microbursts.
decisions: Use per-node soft reservoirs instead of centralized global counters to reduce control-plane writes and latency
Expose reservoir pressure as a soft autoscaler signal with a 30s debounce to prevent oscillation
Provide three pluggable degradation policies for initial rollout: drop, deprioritize-queue, fallback-model. Default to deprioritize-queue for safer user experience
Gate rollout by feature flag and progressive canary with automatic rollback conditions
